title: Garmin Autoland engages after a King Air B200 loses cabin pressure at 23,000 feet and lands it at Broomfield, Colorado, in its first real emergency use
summary: Garmin Autoland engaged when a King Air B200 lost cabin pressure on 20 December 2025 and landed it at Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport, with the two pilots unhurt.
account: On Saturday 20 December 2025 Buffalo River Aviation's Beechcraft Super King Air B200, N479BR, left Aspen-Pitkin County Airport at 1:43 p.m. It carried two pilots and no passengers. At about 23,000 feet it suffered a rapid, uncommanded loss of pressurization. When cabin altitude passed the safe limit, Garmin Autoland engaged automatically. It sent automated emergency broadcasts to air traffic control. The crew chose to leave it engaged. It flew the aircraft to a landing on Runway 30 at Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport, Broomfield, Colorado, shortly after 2 p.m. Nobody was treated. The operator said that the aircraft returned to service the next day. The Federal Aviation Administration said that it was investigating. The National Transportation Safety Board said that it was gathering information. Garmin called it the first use of Autoland from start to finish in an actual emergency. On 27 December 2025 AvBrief reported audio that Max Trescott, a host of the NTSB NewsTalk podcast, recorded while flying nearby. The audio shows that with Autoland engaged the crew could transmit only on the guard frequency and could not switch to the controllers' frequencies. The case database of the National Transportation Safety Board lists no case for the aircraft. On 14 October 2026 Garmin reported that more than 2,500 aircraft carry the system. In 2026 Autoland was certified on four more models, among them the first twin-engine jets. No second real-world activation and no finding by either agency on the Colorado flight had been reported by then.
purpose: Autoland exists to take complete control of an aircraft and land it when the pilot cannot fly. It engages on its own when cabin altitude exceeds a set level. That is what happened here. The two pilots turned out not to be incapacitated, though, and chose to let it finish.

ratings.reason: Two pilots who had lost cabin pressure at 23,000 feet were on the ground in Broomfield within about 35 minutes of departure, untreated and uninjured. They were conscious and could have flown the descent themselves. The benefit is a safe automatic recovery, and no source documents a life saved.

Buffalo River Aviation's aircraft “landed safely without incident”, in the airport spokeswoman's words. No damage is reported, and the operator said that the aircraft returned to service the next day.

ai_role.statement: Autoland engaged itself when cabin altitude exceeded the limit. It declared the emergency to controllers with automated “pilot incapacitation” broadcasts. It flew the descent, approach and landing. The pilots elected to leave it engaged rather than take over. So the landing is the system's work. But the counterfactual, that they could not have landed, is not established. Garmin, the FAA and the operator all call it an automated system. None calls it AI. It is here because the OECD Monitor lists it as an AI system. The Register describes it choosing landing sites from runway length, distance and fuel range.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the OECD Monitor entry and six news reports. The Monitor dates the event 22 December 2025, and every report puts the landing on Saturday 20 December, the date used here. Early reports by AVweb and Denver7, and ABC's headline, said that the pilot was incapacitated. fields.summary: Garmin Autoland engaged when a King Air B200 lost cabin pressure on 20 December 2025 and landed it at Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport, with the two pilots unhurt.
fields.account: On Saturday 20 December 2025 Buffalo River Aviation's Beechcraft Super King Air B200, N479BR, left Aspen-Pitkin County Airport at 1:43 p.m. It carried two pilots and no passengers. At about 23,000 feet it suffered a rapid, uncommanded loss of pressurization. When cabin altitude passed the safe limit, Garmin Autoland engaged automatically. It sent automated emergency broadcasts to air traffic control. The crew chose to leave it engaged. It flew the aircraft to a landing on Runway 30 at Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport, Broomfield, Colorado, shortly after 2 p.m. Nobody was treated. The operator said that the aircraft returned to service the next day. The Federal Aviation Administration said that it was investigating. The National Transportation Safety Board said that it was gathering information. Garmin called it the first use of Autoland from start to finish in an actual emergency. On 27 December 2025 AvBrief reported audio that Max Trescott, a host of the NTSB NewsTalk podcast, recorded while flying nearby. The audio shows that with Autoland engaged the crew could transmit only on the guard frequency and could not switch to the controllers' frequencies. The case database of the National Transportation Safety Board lists no case for the aircraft. On 14 October 2026 Garmin reported that more than 2,500 aircraft carry the system. In 2026 Autoland was certified on four more models, among them the first twin-engine jets. No second real-world activation and no finding by either agency on the Colorado flight had been reported by then.

value.text: Autoland activated after cabin pressure became unsafe and flew the diversion, approach, and landing. The pilots retained the option to take over and deliberately left it engaged.

produced_by: An aircraft fitted with Garmin Autoland. Garmin says more than 1,700 are equipped.
A rapid, uncommanded loss of pressurization that pushed cabin altitude past the system's automatic trigger.
A crew that decided to let the automatic sequence run to touchdown rather than take over.
must_hold: The aircraft remains airworthy. Autoland is a fail-safe for a working aircraft whose pilot cannot fly it, in the words of the journalist CBS quoted.
A suitable airport is in range. The Register describes selection by runway length, distance and fuel range.
Controllers and ground services act on the automated broadcasts, as Broomfield's two fire departments did.
